summary: This applicability statement covers when IPv6 UDP datagrams may use a zero checksum. It gives recommendations and requirements, describes the issues and design principles for UDP tunnels over IPv6, and examines the role of the IPv6 UDP checksum. It also notes constraints on network paths that include middleboxes.

plainLanguage.summary: In IPv4 the IP header itself carries a checksum, so a corrupted packet is thrown away before anyone sees it. IPv6 has no such check, so the UDP checksum is the last line of defence against a packet that has been damaged or delivered to the wrong place. This document explains when a tunnel may skip that check, and what it must do instead to catch the damage.

questions: when is zero udp checksum allowed in ipv6
when is a zero udp checksum allowed in ipv6
why does ipv6 need a udp checksum
can middleboxes drop zero checksum udp
subtitle: When an IPv6 tunnel may skip the UDP checksum, and the rules that make it safe enough.

tldr.problem: IPv6 has no header checksum, so the UDP checksum is the only thing catching misdelivered or corrupted datagrams. Some tunnel protocols, already running over IPv4 with no UDP checksum, want to skip it for IPv6 too.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC says when a zero UDP checksum may be used and sets rules for end hosts, for the protocols that use it and for middleboxes: enable it only per port, keep integrity checks above UDP, probe the path, and fall back to a real checksum.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that works alongside RFC 6935. The RFC's own advice is to try a normal checksummed UDP first and only fall back to a zero checksum when the device makes that impossible.

facts.label: Fast-path bytes seen by some routers

today: RFC 6936 is a Proposed Standard that works alongside RFC 6935, which makes the IPv6 specification itself permit a zero UDP checksum, and the metadata records no document that obsoletes this one. It remains the statement of when that option is safe to use.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The User Datagram Protocol transport is defined for IPv4 and is defined in the IPv6 specification for IPv6 hosts and routers. UDP has a minimal set of features, which has enabled a wide range of applications to use it, but these applications do need to provide many important transport functions on top of UDP. The key difference between UDP usage with IPv4 and IPv6 is that RFC 2460 mandates use of a calculated UDP checksum, that is, a non-zero value, due to the lack of an IPv6 header checksum. The inclusion of the pseudo-header in the checksum computation provides a statistical check that datagrams have been delivered to the intended IPv6 destination node.

The inability to use an IPv6 datagram with a zero UDP checksum has been found to be a real problem for certain classes of application, primarily tunnel applications. This class of application has been deployed with a zero UDP checksum using IPv4. The design of IPv6 raises different issues when considering the safety of using a UDP checksum with IPv6, and these issues can significantly affect applications, whether an endpoint is the intended user or an innocent bystander, that is, when a packet is received by a different endpoint to that intended.

This document identifies a set of issues that must be considered and mitigated to enable safe deployment of IPv6 applications that use a zero UDP checksum, and it defines recommendations and requirements for their use. This usage is expected to have initial deployment issues related to middleboxes, limiting the usability more than desired in the currently deployed Internet. That limitation will be largest initially and will decrease as updates are provided in middleboxes that support the zero UDP checksum for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 has a checksum in the IP header, so damaged packets are dropped early. IPv6 dropped that, so the UDP checksum is the only thing standing between a corrupted packet and the application. Some tunnel protocols, which already run over IPv4 without a UDP checksum, want the same shortcut over IPv6. The document says that is possible, but only under conditions.

sections.title: Why Tunnels Want a Zero Checksum
sections.content:
One increasingly popular use of UDP is as a tunneling protocol, where a tunnel endpoint encapsulates the packets of another protocol inside UDP datagrams and transmits them to another tunnel endpoint. Using UDP as a tunneling protocol is attractive when the payload protocol is not supported by the middleboxes that may exist along the path, because many middleboxes support transmission using UDP. The receiving endpoint decapsulates the UDP datagrams and forwards the original packets contained in the payload. Tunnels establish virtual links that appear to directly connect locations that are distant in the physical Internet topology, and they can be used to create virtual private networks.

A number of tunnel encapsulations deployed over IPv4 have used the UDP transport with a zero checksum, and users of these protocols expect a similar solution for IPv6. A number of tunnel protocols are also currently being defined, such as Automated Multicast Tunnels and the Locator/Identifier Separation Protocol, and these provided several motivations to update IPv6 UDP checksum processing.

The motivations were to reduce forwarding costs, motivated by redundancy present in the encapsulated packet header, because in tunnel encapsulations payload integrity and length verification may be provided by higher-layer encapsulations, often using the IPv4, UDP, UDP-Lite or TCP checksums; to eliminate the need to access the entire packet when a tunnel endpoint forwards the packet; to enhance the ability to traverse and function with middleboxes; and a desire to use the port number space to enable load sharing.

The forwarding cost argument is valid regarding the integrity of a tunneled packet. In some architectures, other mechanisms may also significantly reduce checksum processing costs, for example implementations that have optimized checksum processing algorithms including the use of checksum off-loading, which is readily available for IPv4 packets at high line rates. However, for certain classes of tunnel endpoints this off-loading is not available and is unlikely to become available in the near future.

The currently deployed hardware in many routers uses a fast-path processing that provides only the first n bytes of a packet to the forwarding engine, where typically n is less than or equal to 128. When this design is used to support a tunnel ingress and egress, it prevents fast processing of a transport checksum over an entire, large packet. Enabling checksum calculation over the complete packet can impact router design, performance, energy consumption and cost.

Many paths in the Internet include one or more middleboxes. Large classes of middlebox will handle zero UDP checksum packets but do not support UDP-Lite or the other investigated proposals, including load balancers, equal-cost multipath routing, traffic classifiers, and other functions that read some fields in the UDP headers but do not validate the UDP checksum. There are also middleboxes that either validate or modify the UDP checksum, the two most common classes being firewalls and NATs. It can be reasonably expected that a firewall conforming to RFC 2460 will not regard datagrams with a zero UDP checksum as valid, so use of a zero UDP checksum with IPv6 requires firewalls to be updated before the full utility of the change becomes available.
sections.plainLanguage: Tunnels wrap one protocol inside another. The inner packet often has its own checksum, so computing another one over the outer UDP header is duplicated work. Routers often only look at the first 128 bytes of a packet in hardware, which makes a checksum over a whole large packet slow and expensive. And many middleboxes already pass zero-checksum packets through, because they never look at the checksum. The problem is the other kind of middlebox, the firewalls and NATs that do look.

sections.title: The Alternatives: Checksummed UDP and UDP-Lite
sections.content:
The operation of IPv6 with UDP with a zero checksum is not the same as IPv4 with UDP with a zero checksum, and protocol designers should not be fooled into thinking that the two are the same. Where possible, existing general tunnel encapsulations such as GRE and IP-in-IP should be used. The alternatives to UDP with a zero checksum are UDP with a calculated checksum and UDP-Lite.

UDP with a checksum has the advantage of close to universal support in both endpoints and middleboxes, and it also provides statistical verification of delivery to the intended destination address and port. However, some classes of device have limited support for calculation of a checksum that covers a full datagram, and for these devices that limited support can incur significant processing costs, requiring processing in the router's slow path, and hence can reduce capacity or fail to function.

UDP-Lite has the advantage of using a checksum that can be calculated only over the pseudo-header and the UDP header. This provides a statistical verification of delivery to the intended destination address and port, and the checksum can be calculated without access to the datagram payload. A drawback is that UDP-Lite currently has limited support in both endpoints and middleboxes, which must support the UDP-Lite header type.

IPv6 and UDP with a zero checksum can also be used by nodes that do not permit calculation of a payload checksum, and many existing classes of middlebox do not verify or change the transport checksum, so for those middleboxes IPv6 with a zero UDP checksum is expected to function where UDP-Lite would not. However, support for the zero UDP checksum in middleboxes that do change or verify the checksum is currently limited, and this may result in datagrams with a zero UDP checksum being discarded.

For some sets of constraints, no solution exists. A protocol designer who needs to originate or receive datagrams on a device that cannot efficiently calculate a checksum over a full datagram, and also needs these packets to pass through a middlebox that verifies or changes a UDP checksum but does not support a zero UDP checksum, cannot use the zero UDP checksum method. Similarly, a designer who needs to originate datagrams on a device with UDP-Lite support but needs the packets to pass through a middlebox that does not support UDP-Lite cannot use UDP-Lite. For such cases there is no optimal solution, and the current recommendation is to use or fall back to using UDP with full checksum coverage.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three choices, and none of them wins everywhere. A normal UDP checksum works almost everywhere but is expensive on slow devices. UDP-Lite checks only the header, so it is cheap, but few devices support it. A zero checksum is the cheapest and passes through most middleboxes, but it detects nothing. The document says plainly that for some combinations there is no good answer, and the fallback is a full checksum.

sections.title: What Goes Wrong Without a Checksum
sections.content:
An IPv6 endpoint destination address could be modified in the network, for example by corruption. This is not a concern for IPv4, because the IP header checksum will result in the packet being discarded by the receiving IP stack. When using IPv6, such a modification cannot be detected at the network layer, and detection by a UDP receiver relies on the IPv6 pseudo-header that is incorporated in the transport checksum. There are two possible outcomes: delivery to a destination address that is not in use, in which case the packet will not be delivered, or delivery to a different destination address. The latter modification will normally be detected by the transport checksum, resulting in a silent discard. Without a computed checksum, the packet would be passed to the endpoint port demultiplexing function, and if an application is bound to the associated ports, the packet payload would be passed to the application.

Corruption of an IPv6 source address does not result in the IP packet being delivered to a different endpoint protocol or destination address. If only the source address is corrupted, the datagram will likely be processed in the intended context, although with erroneous origin information. The result then depends on the application or protocol that processes the packet: an application that requires a pre-established context may disregard the datagram as invalid, while other applications may map it to another context.

Corruption of the port information has similar effects. Corruption of the fragmentation information is a further issue, since IPv6 uses a 32-bit fragment identification field against the 16-bit field in IPv4, so a fragment reassembly error is less likely to be detected.

The document also considers a datagram payload being corrupted but still delivered to the intended transport entity, which needs to be either discarded or correctly processed by an application that provides its own integrity checks, and a datagram payload being truncated by corruption of the length field, which needs to be discarded. Using a checksum significantly reduces the impact of errors, reducing the probability of undetected corruption of state and data on both the host stack and the applications using the transport service.
sections.plainLanguage: Without a checksum, a corrupted address can send a packet to the wrong application. The IP layer will not notice, because IPv6 has no header checksum. A corrupted source address is less harmful, since the packet usually reaches the right place but appears to come from the wrong one. A corrupted port number can land the packet on the wrong application. And a corrupted length field can leave the receiver with half a packet. All of these are caught by the UDP checksum when there is one.

sections.title: Validating the Network Path
sections.content:
IP transports designed for use in the general Internet should not assume specific path characteristics. Network protocols may reroute packets, thus changing the set of routers and middleboxes along a path. Transports such as TCP, SCTP and DCCP have been designed to negotiate protocol parameters, adapt to different network path characteristics, and receive feedback to verify that the current path is suited to the intended application. Applications using UDP and UDP-Lite need to provide their own mechanisms to confirm the validity of the current network path.

A zero value in the UDP checksum field is explicitly disallowed in RFC 2460, so any device on the path that has a reason to look beyond the IP header, for example to validate the UDP checksum, will consider such a packet as erroneous or illegal and may discard it, unless the device is updated. Any middlebox that modifies the UDP checksum, for example a NAT that changes the values of the IP and UDP header in such a way that the checksum over the pseudo-header changes value, will need to be updated. Until then, a zero UDP checksum packet is likely to be discarded, either directly in the middlebox or at the destination when a zero UDP checksum has been modified to be non-zero by an incremental update.

A pair of endpoints intending to use the new behaviour will therefore need not only to ensure support at each endpoint, but also to ensure that the path between them will deliver packets with the new behaviour. This may require using negotiation or an explicit mandate. A middlebox may enable zero checksum usage for a particular range of ports. Note that checksum off-loading and operating system design may result in all IPv6 UDP traffic being sent with a calculated checksum, which requires middleboxes configured to enable a zero UDP checksum to continue to work with bidirectional UDP flows that use a zero UDP checksum in only one direction, and therefore they must not maintain separate state for a UDP flow based on its checksum usage.

A sender will need to probe the path to verify the expected behaviour. Path characteristics may change, and usage therefore should be robust and able to detect a failure of the path under normal usage, and should be able to renegotiate. A bidirectional path does not necessarily support the same checksum usage in both the forward and return directions, and receipt of a datagram with a zero UDP checksum does not imply that the remote endpoint can also receive one. This behaviour will require periodic validation of the path, adding complexity to any solution using the new behaviour.
sections.plainLanguage: Just because both ends support zero checksums does not mean the path does. A firewall or NAT in the middle will throw the packets away. So the sender has to test the path, and keep testing it, because the path can change. And a path that works one way may not work the other way, which is why the document asks for periodic validation.

sections.title: Constraints on IPv6 Nodes
sections.content:
This section is an applicability statement that defines requirements and recommendations for the implementation of IPv6 nodes that support the use of a zero value in the checksum field of a UDP datagram. All implementations that support the zero UDP checksum method MUST conform to the requirements defined below.

An IPv6 sending node MAY use a calculated RFC 2460 checksum for all datagrams that it sends, which explicitly permits an interface that supports checksum off-loading to insert an updated UDP checksum value in all UDP datagrams that it forwards. Sending a calculated checksum requires the receiver to also perform the checksum calculation, and checksum off-loading can normally be switched off for a particular interface to ensure that datagrams are sent with a zero UDP checksum. IPv6 nodes SHOULD, by default, NOT allow the zero UDP checksum method for transmission.

IPv6 nodes MUST provide a way for the application or protocol to indicate the set of ports that will be enabled to send datagrams with a zero UDP checksum, and MUST provide a method to allow an application or protocol to indicate that a particular UDP datagram is required to be sent with a UDP checksum. The latter needs to be allowed by the operating system at any time, not just when a socket is established in zero checksum mode, so that keepalive datagrams can be sent with a checksum.

The default IPv6 node receiver behaviour MUST be to discard all IPv6 packets carrying datagrams with a zero UDP checksum. Nodes MUST provide a way for the application or protocol to indicate the set of ports that will be enabled to receive datagrams with a zero UDP checksum, and nodes supporting usage of zero UDP checksums MUST also allow reception using a calculated UDP checksum on all ports configured to allow zero UDP checksum usage.

RFC 2460 specifies that IPv6 nodes SHOULD log received datagrams with a zero UDP checksum, and this remains the case for any datagram received on a port that does not explicitly enable processing of a zero UDP checksum. A port for which the zero UDP checksum has been enabled MUST NOT log the datagram solely because the checksum value is zero. Nodes MAY separately identify received UDP datagrams that are discarded with a zero UDP checksum, but SHOULD NOT add these to the standard log, because the endpoint has not been verified. IPv6 nodes that receive ICMPv6 messages that refer to packets with a zero UDP checksum MUST provide appropriate checks concerning the consistency of the reported packet to verify that the reported packet actually originated from the node, before acting upon the information.
sections.plainLanguage: Ten rules govern a node that supports this. The important ones are that the feature is off by default, that an application has to ask for it by naming the ports it wants, that the receiving side still discards unchecksummed packets unless the application has asked for them too, and that a checksum can still be used on any port even when zero checksums are enabled there. ICMPv6 error messages that quote an unchecksummed packet need extra checking, because the quoted packet might not have come from here.

sections.title: Requirements on Protocols and Tunnels
sections.content:
Before deciding to use the zero UDP checksum and lose the integrity verification provided by non-zero checksumming, a protocol developer should seriously consider whether checksummed UDP packets or UDP-Lite can be used, because IPv6 with a zero UDP checksum is not equivalent in behaviour to IPv4 with zero UDP checksum.

Protocols that enable the use of a zero UDP checksum MUST enable this only for a specific port or port range, and this needs to be enabled at the sending and receiving endpoints for a UDP flow. An integrity mechanism is always RECOMMENDED at the transported protocol layer to ensure that corruption rates of the delivered payload are not increased, for example at the innermost packet of a UDP tunnel. A mechanism that isolates the causes of corruption, such as identifying misdelivery, IPv6 header corruption or tunnel header corruption, also provides additional information about the status of the tunnel, for example to suggest a security attack.

A transported protocol that encapsulates Internet Protocol packets MAY rely on the inner packet integrity checks, provided that the tunnel protocol will not significantly increase the rate of corruption of the inner IP packet. If a significantly increased corruption rate can occur, the tunnel protocol MUST provide an additional integrity verification mechanism. A transported protocol that supports the use of a zero UDP checksum MUST be designed so that corruption of any header information does not result in accumulation of incorrect state for the protocol. A transported protocol with a non-tunnel payload, or one that encapsulates non-IP packets, MUST have a CRC or other mechanism for checking packet integrity.

A transported protocol with control feedback SHOULD be robust to changes in the network path, because the set of middleboxes on a path may vary during the life of an association. Transported protocols SHOULD send keepalive messages with a zero UDP checksum, and an endpoint that discovers an appreciable loss rate for keepalive packets MAY terminate the UDP flow. A protocol with control feedback that can fall back to using UDP with a calculated checksum is expected to be more robust, so keepalive messages SHOULD include both UDP datagrams with a checksum and datagrams with a zero UDP checksum. This enables the remote endpoint to distinguish between a path failure and the dropping of datagrams with a zero UDP checksum.

A middlebox implementation MUST allow forwarding of an IPv6 UDP datagram with both a zero and a standard UDP checksum using the same UDP port. A middlebox MAY configure a restricted set of specific port ranges that forward UDP datagrams with a zero UDP checksum, and MAY drop IPv6 datagrams with a zero UDP checksum that are outside a configured range. When a middlebox forwards an IPv6 UDP flow containing datagrams with both a zero and a standard UDP checksum, the middlebox MUST NOT maintain separate state for flows depending on the value of their UDP checksum field.

Special considerations are required when designing a UDP tunnel protocol where the tunnel ingress or egress may be a router that may not have access to the packet payload. The tunnel ingress and tunnel egress router must both be configured to use a zero UDP checksum, which may include ensuring that hardware checksum off-loading is disabled. The tunnel operator must ensure that middleboxes on the network path are updated to support use of a zero UDP checksum. A tunnel egress should implement appropriate security techniques to protect from overload, including source address filtering to prevent traffic injection by an attacker and rate-limiting of any packets that incur additional processing.
sections.plainLanguage: On the protocol side there are ten more rules. A tunnel must turn the feature on only for its own ports, and must keep its own integrity checks, either by relying on the inner packet's checksum or by adding one of its own. Corrupted headers must not leave the tunnel in a wrong state. Keepalives should be sent both with and without a checksum, so the far end can tell a broken path from a middlebox dropping unchecksummed packets. And a middlebox must not treat a zero-checksum flow and a checksummed flow as two different flows.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Transport checksums provide the first stage of protection for the stack, although they cannot be considered authentication mechanisms. These checks are also desirable to ensure that packet counters correctly log actual activity, and they can be used to detect unusual behaviours.

Depending on the hardware design, the processing requirements may differ for tunnels that have a zero UDP checksum and those that calculate a checksum. This processing overhead may need to be considered when deciding whether to enable a tunnel. It can become a security risk for designs that can handle a significantly larger number of packets with zero UDP checksums compared to datagrams with a non-zero checksum, such as a tunnel egress. An attacker could attempt to inject non-zero checksummed UDP packets into a tunnel that is forwarding zero checksum UDP packets and cause overload in the processing of the non-zero checksums, for example if it happens in a router's slow path. Protection mechanisms should therefore be employed when this threat exists, including source-address filtering and throttling the amount of non-zero checksum traffic.

Transmission of IPv6 packets with a zero UDP checksum could reveal additional information to help an on-path attacker identify the operating system or configuration of a sending node. There is a need to probe the network path to determine whether the current path supports the use of IPv6 packets with a zero UDP checksum, and if the probing mechanism is visible in the network, for example when not using IPsec in encryption mode, it could reveal the type of tunnel being used.

IP-in-IP or GRE tunnels offer good traversal of middleboxes that have not been designed for security, but firewalls may be expected to be configured to block general tunnels, because they present a large attack surface. This applicability statement therefore permits the method to be enabled only for specific port ranges. When the zero UDP checksum mode is enabled for a range of ports, nodes and middleboxes must forward received UDP datagrams that have either a calculated checksum or a zero checksum.
sections.plainLanguage: A checksum is not authentication, but it is the first line of defence, and dropping it means more work for the endpoint to do. There is also an asymmetry to watch: a tunnel that forwards unchecksummed packets cheaply could be overwhelmed by an attacker sending expensive checksummed packets into it. Rate limiting and source address filtering are the stated protections. And a zero checksum tells an on-path observer something about the sender's software, which is a small leak worth knowing about.

viz.caption: The three ways to carry a tunnel over IPv6

cells: The whole datagram, plus the pseudo-header, so it confirms the destination address and port.
Almost everywhere: endpoints and middleboxes both support it.
Expensive on devices that cannot compute a checksum over a full datagram.
Only the pseudo-header and the UDP header, so it confirms the destination address and port.
Only where the UDP-Lite header type is supported.
Limited support in endpoints and middleboxes.
Devices that cannot compute a payload checksum, and middleboxes that do not verify or change the checksum.
Support in middleboxes that do change or verify the checksum is currently limited, and datagrams may be discarded.

viz.caption: The rules a node that supports zero checksums must follow

items.title: Off by default
items.text: Nodes SHOULD, by default, NOT allow the zero UDP checksum method for transmission.

items.title: Sending is per port
items.text: There must be a way for the application to name the set of ports that may send with a zero checksum.

items.title: Receiving is per port
items.text: The default receiver behaviour is to discard all packets carrying a zero UDP checksum, and an application must opt in by port.

items.title: A real checksum is still allowed
items.text: A node must let the application ask for one particular datagram to carry a checksum, at any time, and must accept checksummed datagrams on ports enabled for zero checksums.

items.title: No separate flow state
items.text: Middleboxes must not keep separate state for a flow based on whether its checksum is zero.

items.title: ICMPv6 needs care
items.text: An ICMPv6 message that quotes an unchecksummed packet must be checked for consistency before it is acted on.
